idiom_name: hand-written struct satisfying the service interface (optionally httptest server or mockgen)
implementation_notes: Go needs no framework for this pattern: interface satisfaction is implicit, so a small struct with the same method set is the stand-in and a compile-time assertion such as var _ PriceService = (*fakePriceService)(nil) keeps it honest when the contract changes. When the service is spoken to over HTTP the idiomatic seam is the network itself - httptest.NewServer serves canned responses from a handler and the server's URL is handed to the real client, so serialization and status handling run for real. Reach for mockgen only with wide interfaces where implementing every method by hand is noise.
pitfalls: Embedding the interface in the fake to avoid implementing every method compiles and then panics with a nil-pointer dereference when an unimplemented operation is called; assert the full method set instead.
A fake shared across parallel subtests races on its recording state: guard it with a mutex or give each subtest its own instance.
Returning a pointer to shared fixture data lets the client mutate it, so later assertions observe the mutated value.

variants.name: httptest.NewServer standing in for the whole service
variants.implementation_notes: Instead of substituting the client's collaborator, stand up a real local HTTP endpoint and point the production client at its URL: the client's request construction, decoding and error handling all execute, only the remote process is missing. This is the closest a pure-Go test gets to the real service, and it needs no doubles at all.
pitfalls: The fake server answers whatever the handler returns, so it will happily accept a request the real service would reject: assert method, path and headers when the wire contract matters.
Forgetting defer srv.Close() leaks a listener per test and eventually exhausts the test process's file descriptors.

variants.name: mockgen-generated mock with expectations
variants.implementation_notes: mockgen reads the interface - from source, an archive or a package - and generates a mock with typed expectation helpers, so wide interfaces cost nothing to double and the recorder verifies call counts and argument matchers for you. Prefer it when the interface is large or when several packages need the same mock; keep hand-written fakes for the small, behaviour-carrying doubles, because generated expectations are easy to over-specify.
variants.code_sketch:
ctrl := gomock.NewController(t)
prices := NewMockPriceService(ctrl)
prices.EXPECT().
	Price(gomock.Any(), "A-1").
	Return(9.99, nil).
	Times(1)

checkout := NewCheckout(prices)
pitfalls: Expectations default to exactly once (Times(1)), so a legitimate repeat call fails the test unless the count is stated.
Generated mocks live in a mock package that must be regenerated when the interface changes; a stale mock package is the Go flavour of stub drift.
